claim: VEGFR2 (also known as KDR or FLK1) is expressed specifically in the CA3 region in the developing hippocampus
source: Here, we show that in the developing hippocampus VEGFR2 (also known as KDR or FLK1) is expressed specifically in the CA3 region and it is required for dendritic arborization and spine morphogenesis in hippocampal neurons.
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1A,B and confirmed by VEGFR2-GFP knock-in mouse in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A

claim: VEGFR2 is required for dendritic arborization in hippocampal neurons
source: Here, we show that in the developing hippocampus VEGFR2 (also known as KDR or FLK1) is expressed specifically in the CA3 region and it is required for dendritic arborization and spine morphogenesis in hippocampal neurons.
evidence: Demonstrated by reduced dendritic length, branch points, and complexity in Nes-cre Kdrlox/- mice shown in Figure 1C-G

claim: VEGFR2 is required for spine morphogenesis in hippocampal neurons
source: Here, we show that in the developing hippocampus VEGFR2 (also known as KDR or FLK1) is expressed specifically in the CA3 region and it is required for dendritic arborization and spine morphogenesis in hippocampal neurons.
evidence: Supported by data showing reduced spine density and head size in Nes-cre Kdrlox/- mice in Figure 2A-D

claim: Mice lacking VEGFR2 in neurons (Nes-cre Kdrlox/-) show decreased dendritic arbors and spines
source: Mice lacking VEGFR2 in neurons (Nes-cre Kdrlox/-) show decreased dendritic arbors and spines as well as a reduction in long-term potentiation (LTP) at the associational-commissural – CA3 synapses.
evidence: Demonstrated by quantitative analysis in Figure 1D-G for dendrites and Figure 2A-D for spines

claim: Mice lacking VEGFR2 in neurons show a reduction in long-term potentiation (LTP) at the associational-commissural – CA3 synapses
source: Mice lacking VEGFR2 in neurons (Nes-cre Kdrlox/-) show decreased dendritic arbors and spines as well as a reduction in long-term potentiation (LTP) at the associational-commissural – CA3 synapses.
evidence: Shown by electrophysiological recordings in Figure 2E-G demonstrating reduced LTP in Nes-cre Kdrlox/- mice

claim: VEGFR2 internalization is required for VEGF-induced spine maturation
source: Mechanistically, VEGFR2 internalization is required for VEGF-induced spine maturation.
evidence: Demonstrated by dynasore inhibition experiments in Figure 3D-E showing that blocking internalization abolishes VEGF-induced spine maturation

claim: EphrinB2 controls VEGFR2 internalization in neurons
source: In analogy to endothelial cells, ephrinB2 controls VEGFR2 internalization in neurons.
evidence: Shown by PLA experiments in Figure 5A-B demonstrating impaired VEGF-induced VEGFR2 internalization in ephrinB2 deficient neurons

claim: VEGFR2-ephrinB2 compound mice (Nes-cre Kdrlox/+ Efnb2lox/+) show reduced dendritic branching
source: VEGFR2-ephrinB2 compound mice (Nes-cre Kdrlox/+ Efnb2lox/+) show reduced dendritic branching, reduced spine head size and impaired LTP.
evidence: Demonstrated by morphological analysis in Figure 6A-E showing reduced total dendritic length, branch points, and intersections

claim: VEGFR2-ephrinB2 compound mice show reduced spine head size
source: VEGFR2-ephrinB2 compound mice (Nes-cre Kdrlox/+ Efnb2lox/+) show reduced dendritic branching, reduced spine head size and impaired LTP.
evidence: Shown by spine morphology analysis in Figure 6F-I demonstrating reduced spine density and head size

claim: VEGFR2-ephrinB2 compound mice show impaired LTP
source: VEGFR2-ephrinB2 compound mice (Nes-cre Kdrlox/+ Efnb2lox/+) show reduced dendritic branching, reduced spine head size and impaired LTP.
evidence: Demonstrated by electrophysiological recordings in Figure 7A-B showing significantly reduced LTP in compound mice

claim: CA3 neurons are generated around E14.5
source: CA3 neurons are generated around E14.5 and CA1 neurons one day later at E15.5 (Grove, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Grove, 1999

claim: CA1 neurons are generated at E15.5
source: CA3 neurons are generated around E14.5 and CA1 neurons one day later at E15.5 (Grove, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Grove, 1999

claim: Neurogenesis of the dentate gyrus granule cell starts shortly before birth
source: Neurogenesis of the dentate gyrus granule cell starts shortly before birth, peaks in the first postnatal week and continues until adulthood.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of hippocampal development

claim: Neurogenesis of the dentate gyrus granule cell peaks in the first postnatal week
source: Neurogenesis of the dentate gyrus granule cell starts shortly before birth, peaks in the first postnatal week and continues until adulthood.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of hippocampal development

claim: Neurogenesis of the dentate gyrus granule cell continues until adulthood
source: Neurogenesis of the dentate gyrus granule cell starts shortly before birth, peaks in the first postnatal week and continues until adulthood.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of hippocampal development

claim: Post-migratory neuroblasts start to develop their processes upon arrival in their appropriate layer
source: Upon arrival of hippocampal cells in their appropriate layer, the post-migratory neuroblasts start to develop their processes (Altman and Bayer, 1990).
evidence: Supported by citation to Altman and Bayer, 1990

claim: During late neonatal and early postnatal brain development, dendritic arbors are highly dynamic and undergo continuous changes in shape and orientation
source: During late neonatal and early postnatal brain development, dendritic arbors are highly dynamic and undergo continuous changes in shape and orientation (Dailey and Smith, 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dailey and Smith, 1996

claim: Neurons extend and retract branches as they mature
source: Neurons extend and retract branches as they mature and only a subset of the original dendrites become stabilized in the mature brain.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of neuronal development

claim: Only a subset of the original dendrites become stabilized in the mature brain
source: Neurons extend and retract branches as they mature and only a subset of the original dendrites become stabilized in the mature brain.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of neuronal development

claim: An early dynamic period is essential for proper wiring, synapse formation and the establishment of neural circuits
source: Such an early dynamic period is essential for proper wiring, synapse formation and the establishment of neural circuits (Wong and Wong, 2000; Matsuzaki et al., 2001; Koleske, 2013)
evidence: Supported by citations to Wong and Wong, 2000; Matsuzaki et al., 2001; Koleske, 2013

claim: Dendrite stabilization and synapse formation are strongly coupled during early dynamic period
source: During this time, dendrite stabilization and synapse formation are strongly coupled.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of neuronal development and supported by citation to Koleske, 2013

claim: As circuits mature further in juvenile stages, structural plasticity decreases and dendrites become stabilized
source: As circuits mature further in juvenile stages, structural plasticity decreases and dendrites become stabilized, whereas dendritic spines stay dynamic and change in shape (Engert and Bonhoeffer, 1999; Trachtenberg et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Engert and Bonhoeffer, 1999; Trachtenberg et al., 2002

claim: Dendritic spines stay dynamic and change in shape as circuits mature in juvenile stages
source: As circuits mature further in juvenile stages, structural plasticity decreases and dendrites become stabilized, whereas dendritic spines stay dynamic and change in shape (Engert and Bonhoeffer, 1999; Trachtenberg et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Engert and Bonhoeffer, 1999; Trachtenberg et al., 2002

claim: BDNF and its receptor TrkB are involved in dendritic outgrowth and stabilization
source: Extrinsic factors, such as BDNF and its receptor TrkB, are involved in dendritic outgrowth and stabilization (Horch and Katz, 2002; Gorski et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Horch and Katz, 2002; Gorski et al., 2003

claim: Semaphorin 3A can act as chemorepellant on axons and as a chemoattractant on dendrites of cortical pyramidal neurons
source: Semaphorin 3A can act as chemorepellant on axons and as a chemoattractant on dendrites of cortical pyramidal neurons (Polleux et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Polleux et al., 2000

claim: GRIP1 and 14-3-3 proteins control kinesin-1 motor attachment during microtubule-based transport thereby regulating delivery of cargos to dendrites and spines
source: Thus, glutamate receptor interacting protein 1 (GRIP1) and 14-3-3 proteins control kinesin-1 motor attachment during microtubule-based transport thereby regulating delivery of cargos to dendrites and spines (Geiger et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Geiger et al., 2014

claim: Vascular and nervous systems share common signaling pathways during development
source: Vascular and nervous systems share common signaling pathways during development.
evidence: Supported by citations to reviews (Carmeliet and Tessier-Lavigne, 2005; Tam and Watts, 2010; Paredes et al., 2018)

claim: VEGF and its receptor VEGFR2 are well known for their angiogenic function in the vascular system
source: VEGF and its receptor VEGFR2 (encoded by the gene Kdr) are well known for their angiogenic function in the vascular system.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge of VEGF/VEGFR2 function

claim: EphrinB2 controls VEGFR2 signaling by regulating its internalization in endothelial cells
source: Previously, our laboratory described the molecular mechanism for the function of the neuronal guidance molecule ephrinB2 during vascular development (Sawamiphak et al., 2010). EphrinB2 controls VEGFR2 signaling by regulating its internalization in endothelial cells.
evidence: Supported by citation to Sawamiphak et al., 2010

claim: The interaction between ephrinB2 and VEGFR2 is crucial for proper spatial activation and downstream signaling of VEGFR2
source: This interaction is crucial for proper spatial activation and downstream signaling of VEGFR2 and is required for VEGF-induced tip cell filopodial extension in the developing retina.
evidence: Based on previous work cited (Sawamiphak et al., 2010)

claim: The ephrinB2-VEGFR2 interaction is required for VEGF-induced tip cell filopodial extension in the developing retina
source: This interaction is crucial for proper spatial activation and downstream signaling of VEGFR2 and is required for VEGF-induced tip cell filopodial extension in the developing retina.
evidence: Based on previous work cited (Sawamiphak et al., 2010)

claim: Specialized endothelial tip cells at the forefront of growing vessels that extend filopodial extensions are comparable to axonal growth cones
source: In this sense, the specialized endothelial tip cells at the forefront of growing vessels that extend filopodial extensions are comparable to axonal growth cones.
evidence: Based on inference from structural and functional similarities

claim: VEGF and its receptors function in neuronal cells
source: In agreement with the molecular parallelism between the vascular and nervous system, VEGF and its receptors, which were originally described as key regulators of angiogenesis, also function in neuronal cells (reviewed in Ruiz de Almodovar et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to review by Ruiz de Almodovar et al., 2009

claim: VEGF regulates adult hippocampal synaptic plasticity
source: For example, some studies have attributed roles for VEGF in regulating adult hippocampal synaptic plasticity (Kim et al., 2008; Licht et al., 2011; De Rossi et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to Kim et al., 2008; Licht et al., 2011; De Rossi et al., 2016

claim: VEGF modulates the arborization of dendrites of newly integrated interneurons in the olfactory bulb during adult neurogenesis
source: or in modulating the arborization of dendrites of newly integrated interneurons in the olfactory bulb during adult neurogenesis (Licht et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Licht et al., 2010

claim: VEGF effects in axon guidance are mediated via VEGFR2
source: VEGF effects in axon guidance have been shown to be mediated via VEGFR2 (Ruiz de Almodovar et al., 2011) and via Neuropilin1 (Erskine et al., 2011) depending on the neuronal type.
evidence: Supported by citation to Ruiz de Almodovar et al., 2011

claim: VEGF effects in axon guidance are mediated via Neuropilin1 depending on the neuronal type
source: VEGF effects in axon guidance have been shown to be mediated via VEGFR2 (Ruiz de Almodovar et al., 2011) and via Neuropilin1 (Erskine et al., 2011) depending on the neuronal type.
evidence: Supported by citation to Erskine et al., 2011

claim: Immunohistochemistry in the developing hippocampus at postnatal day 10 (P10) showed high expression of VEGFR2 in the vessels
source: Immunohistochemistry in the developing hippocampus at postnatal day 10 (P10) showed, as expected, high expression of VEGFR2 in the vessels, but interestingly also specifically in CA3 pyramidal neurons (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1A,B

claim: Immunohistochemistry in the developing hippocampus at postnatal day 10 (P10) showed high expression of VEGFR2 specifically in CA3 pyramidal neurons
source: Immunohistochemistry in the developing hippocampus at postnatal day 10 (P10) showed, as expected, high expression of VEGFR2 in the vessels, but interestingly also specifically in CA3 pyramidal neurons (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1A,B

claim: The VEGFR2 expression pattern in CA3 pyramidal neurons was confirmed by using a knock-in mouse expressing VEGFR2-GFP
source: This expression pattern was confirmed by using a knock-in mouse expressing VEGFR2-GFP, where exon 1 of the Kdr gene is replaced by GFP (Ema et al., 2006), and therefore GFP labeling reflects VEGFR2 endogenous expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Demonstrated by VEGFR2-GFP expression data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A

claim: At P10, the hippocampus undergoes remodeling of dendrites and spine morphogenesis
source: Noteworthy, at this developmental stage, the hippocampus undergoes remodeling of dendrites and spine morphogenesis (Grove, 1999; Koleske, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Grove, 1999; Koleske, 2013

claim: Nervous system specific VEGFR2 knockout mice are heterozygous for Nestin-cre and carry one conditional 'floxed' allele and one null Kdr allele
source: The resulting nervous system specific VEGFR2 knockout mice are heterozygous for Nestin-cre and are carrying one conditional 'floxed' allele and one null Kdr allele (Nes-cre Kdrlox/-).
evidence: Description of the genetic composition of the mouse model

claim: In Nes-cre Kdrlox/- mice, the absence of VEGFR2 expression in neurons was validated by PCR, RT-qPCR and immunohistochemistry
source: In the Nes-cre Kdrlox/- mice, the absence of VEGFR2 expression in neurons was validated by PCR, RT-qPCR and immunohistochemistry (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–D and De Rossi et al., 2016).
evidence: Demonstrated by validation experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–D

claim: In nervous system specific knockout mice, VEGFR2 expression is abrogated in neurons but is still normally expressed in vessels
source: In this nervous system specific knockout mice, VEGFR2 expression is abrogated in neurons but is still normally expressed in vessels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, arrowheads) enabling us to address cell-autonomous functions of VEGFR2 in neurons.
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D showing vessel expression

claim: Cells of Nes-cre Kdrlox/- mice showed a reduced total dendritic length
source: Cells of Nes-cre Kdrlox/- mice showed a reduced total dendritic length (Figure 1D).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification shown in Figure 1D

claim: 3D Sholl analysis revealed a significant reduction in the number of branch points in Nes-cre Kdrlox/- mice compared to control littermates
source: 3D Sholl analysis revealed a significant reduction in the number of branch points (Figure 1E) and number of intersections (Figure 1F,G) in Nes-cre Kdrlox/- mice compared to control littermates.
evidence: Demonstrated by Sholl analysis data in Figure 1E

claim: 3D Sholl analysis revealed a significant reduction in the number of intersections in Nes-cre Kdrlox/- mice compared to control littermates
source: 3D Sholl analysis revealed a significant reduction in the number of branch points (Figure 1E) and number of intersections (Figure 1F,G) in Nes-cre Kdrlox/- mice compared to control littermates.
evidence: Demonstrated by Sholl analysis data in Figure 1F,G

claim: Nes-cre Kdrlox/- mice showed a significant reduction in spine density
source: Nes-cre Kdrlox/- mice showed a significant reduction in spine density and head size (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: Demonstrated by spine analysis data in Figure 2B

claim: Nes-cre Kdrlox/- mice showed a significant reduction in spine head size
source: Nes-cre Kdrlox/- mice showed a significant reduction in spine density and head size (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: Demonstrated by spine analysis data in Figure 2C

claim: The distribution of spine head size was different in the Nes-cre Kdrlox/- mice compared to control littermates
source: Additionally, the distribution of spine head size was different in the Nes-cre Kdrlox/- mice compared to control littermates.
evidence: Demonstrated by distribution analysis in Figure 2D

claim: Nes-cre Kdrlox/- mice possessed a higher fraction of small spine heads
source: Nes-cre Kdrlox/- mice possessed a higher fraction of small spine heads, whereas the proportion of larger spines was decreased (Figure 2D).
evidence: Demonstrated by distribution analysis in Figure 2D

claim: The proportion of larger spines was decreased in Nes-cre Kdrlox/- mice
source: Nes-cre Kdrlox/- mice possessed a higher fraction of small spine heads, whereas the proportion of larger spines was decreased (Figure 2D).
evidence: Demonstrated by distribution analysis in Figure 2D

claim: Activation of VEGFR2 by its ligand VEGF led to an increase in the number of mature spines in hippocampal neurons in culture
source: Activation of VEGFR2 by its ligand VEGF led to an increase in the number of mature spines in hippocampal neurons in culture (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), indicating that VEGF has a direct and supportive effect on spine formation.
evidence: Demonstrated by in vitro experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: VEGF has a direct and supportive effect on spine formation
source: Activation of VEGFR2 by its ligand VEGF led to an increase in the number of mature spines in hippocampal neurons in culture (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), indicating that VEGF has a direct and supportive effect on spine formation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that VEGF stimulation increases mature spines shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Loss of VEGFR2 results in dendritic spines with a reduced head size and an increased fraction of immature filopodia
source: Taken together, loss of VEGFR2 results in dendritic spines with a reduced head size and an increased fraction of immature filopodia, whereas activation of VEGF signaling leads to the formation of mature dendritic spines.
evidence: Summary of findings from Figure 2A-D showing spine phenotypes in knockout mice

claim: Activation of VEGF signaling leads to the formation of mature dendritic spines
source: Taken together, loss of VEGFR2 results in dendritic spines with a reduced head size and an increased fraction of immature filopodia, whereas activation of VEGF signaling leads to the formation of mature dendritic spines.
evidence: Summary of findings from Figure 2—figure supplement 1 showing VEGF-induced spine maturation

claim: In endothelial cells, VEGF stimulation leads to the activation of a variety of downstream signaling pathways
source: In endothelial cells, VEGF stimulation leads to the activation of a variety of downstream signaling pathways (reviewed in Olsson et al., 2006)
evidence: Supported by citation to review by Olsson et al., 2006

claim: The internalization of VEGFR2 is required for the phosphorylation of the receptor and the activation of the downstream signaling events in endothelial cells
source: and the internalization of its receptor VEGFR2 is required for the phosphorylation of the receptor and the activation of the downstream signaling events (Lampugnani et al., 2006; Sawamiphak et al., 2010; Nakayama et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lampugnani et al., 2006; Sawamiphak et al., 2010; Nakayama et al., 2013

claim: VEGF stimulation led to a significant increase in VEGFR2 localization in early endosomes in hippocampal neurons
source: Double-labeling with the early endosomal marker EEA1 enabled the analysis of endocytosed VEGFR2 and showed a significant increase in VEGFR2 localization in early endosomes upon VEGF stimulation (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: Demonstrated by PLA experiments shown in Figure 3A,B

claim: In untreated neurons, VEGF stimulation led to the phosphorylation of VEGFR2
source: In untreated neurons, VEGF stimulation led to the phosphorylation of VEGFR2 whereas VEGFR2 activation was impaired when neurons were treated with dynasore (Figure 3C).
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot analysis shown in Figure 3C

claim: VEGFR2 activation was impaired when neurons were treated with dynasore
source: In untreated neurons, VEGF stimulation led to the phosphorylation of VEGFR2 whereas VEGFR2 activation was impaired when neurons were treated with dynasore (Figure 3C).
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot analysis shown in Figure 3C

claim: VEGF can activate Src kinase in migrating cerebellar granule cells
source: It has been shown that VEGF can activate Src kinase in migrating cerebellar granule cells (Meissirel et al., 2011) and in commissural neurons (Ruiz de Almodovar et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Meissirel et al., 2011

claim: VEGF can activate Src kinase in commissural neurons
source: It has been shown that VEGF can activate Src kinase in migrating cerebellar granule cells (Meissirel et al., 2011) and in commissural neurons (Ruiz de Almodovar et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ruiz de Almodovar et al., 2011

claim: Akt kinase was identified as a downstream partner of VEGF signaling promoting endothelial cell survival
source: Additionally, Akt kinase was identified as a downstream partner of VEGF signaling promoting endothelial cell survival (Gerber et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gerber et al., 1998

claim: Src family kinases are involved in structural and synaptic plasticity
source: As Src family kinases and Akt are additionally both involved in structural and synaptic plasticity (Lu et al., 1998; Jaworski et al., 2005; Kumar et al., 2005; Babus et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citations to Lu et al., 1998; Jaworski et al., 2005; Kumar et al., 2005; Babus et al., 2011

claim: Akt is involved in structural and synaptic plasticity
source: As Src family kinases and Akt are additionally both involved in structural and synaptic plasticity (Lu et al., 1998; Jaworski et al., 2005; Kumar et al., 2005; Babus et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citations to Lu et al., 1998; Jaworski et al., 2005; Kumar et al., 2005; Babus et al., 2011

claim: VEGF stimulation led to the activation of Src family kinases in hippocampal neurons
source: In analogy with VEGF signaling in endothelial cells, we found that VEGF stimulation led to the activation of Src family kinases and Akt in hippocampal neurons (Figure 3C).
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot analysis shown in Figure 3C

claim: VEGF stimulation led to the activation of Akt in hippocampal neurons
source: In analogy with VEGF signaling in endothelial cells, we found that VEGF stimulation led to the activation of Src family kinases and Akt in hippocampal neurons (Figure 3C).
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot analysis shown in Figure 3C

claim: VEGF-induced Src family kinases activation was impaired in dynasore treated neurons
source: Endocytosis was also required for VEGFR2 downstream signaling as VEGF-induced Src family kinases and Akt activation was impaired in dynasore treated neurons (Figure 3C).
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot analysis shown in Figure 3C

claim: VEGF-induced Akt activation was impaired in dynasore treated neurons
source: Endocytosis was also required for VEGFR2 downstream signaling as VEGF-induced Src family kinases and Akt activation was impaired in dynasore treated neurons (Figure 3C).
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot analysis shown in Figure 3C

claim: Treatment with dynasore impaired the VEGF-induced maturation of spines
source: GFP-transfected hippocampal wild type neurons were pretreated with dynasore before stimulation with VEGF. The cells were fixed at 14 DIV and spine density was analyzed. Treatment with dynasore impaired the VEGF-induced maturation of spines (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: Demonstrated by spine analysis in dynasore-treated neurons shown in Figure 3D,E

claim: Internalization of VEGFR2 is required for activation and downstream signaling of the receptor leading to the maturation of dendritic spines in hippocampal neurons
source: These results indicate that internalization of VEGFR2 is required for activation and downstream signaling of the receptor leading to the maturation of dendritic spines in hippocampal neurons.
evidence: Inferred from dynasore inhibition experiments showing impaired VEGFR2 activation and spine maturation in Figure 3

claim: EphrinBs are highly expressed in hippocampal neurons
source: EphrinBs are highly expressed in hippocampal neurons and play important roles in hippocampal synaptic plasticity (Grunwald et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Grunwald et al., 2004

claim: EphrinBs play important roles in hippocampal synaptic plasticity
source: EphrinBs are highly expressed in hippocampal neurons and play important roles in hippocampal synaptic plasticity (Grunwald et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Grunwald et al., 2004

claim: Pulldown of endogenous ephrinB2 with the ectodomain of its specific cognate receptor EphB4 fused to Fc showed endogenous VEGFR2 binding
source: Pulldown of endogenous ephrinB2 with the ectodomain of its specific cognate receptor EphB4 fused to Fc (EphB4-Fc) showed endogenous VEGFR2 binding (Figure 4A), suggesting that VEGFR2 and ephrinB2 physically form a complex in hippocampal neurons.
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiment shown in Figure 4A

claim: VEGFR2 and ephrinB2 physically form a complex in hippocampal neurons
source: Pulldown of endogenous ephrinB2 with the ectodomain of its specific cognate receptor EphB4 fused to Fc (EphB4-Fc) showed endogenous VEGFR2 binding (Figure 4A), suggesting that VEGFR2 and ephrinB2 physically form a complex in hippocampal neurons.
evidence: Inferred from co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 4A showing physical interaction

claim: VEGFR2/ephrinB2 PLA punctae were found on spine heads and necks along the dendrites of hippocampal neurons
source: Interestingly, VEGFR2/ephrinB2 PLA punctae were found on spine heads and necks along the dendrites of hippocampal neurons (Figure 4B)
evidence: Demonstrated by PLA experiments shown in Figure 4B

claim: Double-staining with the postsynaptic marker PSD95 revealed localization of VEGFR2/ephrinB2 PLA punctae to the postsynaptic side
source: and a double-staining with the postsynaptic marker PSD95 revealed localization of PLA punctae to the postsynaptic side (Figure 4C).
evidence: Demonstrated by PLA and PSD95 co-staining shown in Figure 4C

claim: VEGF treatment significantly increased the co-localization of ephrinB2-VEGFR2 complex in early endosomes
source: VEGF treatment significantly increased the co-localization of ephrinB2-VEGFR2 complex in early endosomes (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: Demonstrated by PLA and EEA1 co-localization analysis shown in Figure 4D,E

claim: The VEGFR2-ephrinB2 complex is internalized and translocated to early endosomes upon VEGF binding
source: These results show that the VEGFR2-ephrinB2 complex is internalized and translocated to early endosomes upon VEGF binding.
evidence: Inferred from PLA experiments showing increased co-localization with EEA1 after VEGF treatment in Figure 4D,E

claim: In control neurons, stimulation with VEGF significantly increased the fraction of VEGFR2 punctae that were co-localized with early endosomes
source: In control neurons, stimulation with VEGF significantly increased the fraction of VEGFR2 punctae that were co-localized with early endosomes (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: Demonstrated by PLA experiments in control neurons shown in Figure 5A,B

claim: In neurons lacking ephrinB2, VEGF stimulation had no significant effect on VEGFR2 translocation to EEA1-positive endosomes
source: In contrast, in neurons lacking ephrinB2, VEGF stimulation had no significant effect of VEGFR2 translocation to EEA1-positve endosomes (Figure 5A,B), indicating that VEGFR2 internalization is regulated by ephrinB2 in hippocampal neurons.
evidence: Demonstrated by PLA experiments in ephrinB2 knockout neurons shown in Figure 5A,B

claim: VEGFR2 internalization is regulated by ephrinB2 in hippocampal neurons
source: In contrast, in neurons lacking ephrinB2, VEGF stimulation had no significant effect of VEGFR2 translocation to EEA1-positve endosomes (Figure 5A,B), indicating that VEGFR2 internalization is regulated by ephrinB2 in hippocampal neurons.
evidence: Inferred from experiments showing impaired VEGFR2 internalization in ephrinB2 knockout neurons in Figure 5A,B

claim: VEGF stimulation led to a strong increase in the number of spines in control cultures
source: VEGF stimulation led to a strong increase in the number of spines in control cultures, an effect that was abolished in the ephrinB2 knockout cultures (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: Demonstrated by spine analysis in control neurons shown in Figure 5C,D

claim: The VEGF-induced increase in spine number was abolished in ephrinB2 knockout cultures
source: VEGF stimulation led to a strong increase in the number of spines in control cultures, an effect that was abolished in the ephrinB2 knockout cultures (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: Demonstrated by spine analysis in ephrinB2 knockout neurons shown in Figure 5C,D

claim: Hippocampal neurons stimulated with EphB4 showed a significant increase in mature spines
source: In agreement with the function of EphrinB2 in spine morphogenesis, hippocampal neurons stimulated with its cognate receptor EphB4 also showed a significant increase in mature spines (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by spine analysis after EphB4 stimulation shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: In VEGFR2-ephrinB2 compound mice the total dendritic length was strongly decreased compared to the littermate controls
source: VEGFR2-ephrinB2 compound mice (Nes-cre Kdrlox/+ Efnb2lox/+) were crossed to Thy1-GFP mice and the morphology of CA3 pyramidal neurons was analyzed at P10. In VEGFR2-ephrinB2 compound mice the total dendritic length was strongly decreased compared to the littermate controls (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: Demonstrated by dendritic length analysis in compound mice shown in Figure 6A,B

claim: 3D sholl analysis showed a reduced branching pattern with a reduction in the number of branch-points in ephrinB2-VEGFR2 double-heterozygous compound mice
source: Additionally, 3D sholl analysis showed a reduced branching pattern with a reduction in the number of branch-points (Figure 6C) and number of intersections (Figure 6D,E) in the ephrinB2-VEGFR2 double-heterozygous compound mice as compared to Nes-cre negative control littermates.
evidence: Demonstrated by Sholl analysis in compound mice shown in Figure 6C

claim: 3D sholl analysis showed a reduced branching pattern with a reduction in the number of intersections in ephrinB2-VEGFR2 double-heterozygous compound mice
source: Additionally, 3D sholl analysis showed a reduced branching pattern with a reduction in the number of branch-points (Figure 6C) and number of intersections (Figure 6D,E) in the ephrinB2-VEGFR2 double-heterozygous compound mice as compared to Nes-cre negative control littermates.
evidence: Demonstrated by Sholl analysis in compound mice shown in Figure 6D,E

claim: Single heterozygous VEGFR2 and ephrinB2 mice showed a branching pattern that was undistinguishable from controls
source: Importantly, single heterozygous VEGFR2 and ephrinB2 mice (Nes-cre Kdrlox/+ and Nes-cre Efnb2lox/+) showed a branching pattern that was undistinguishable from controls (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the phenotype observed arises from the genetic interaction of both pathways.
evidence: Demonstrated by dendritic analysis in single heterozygous mice shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: The phenotype observed in compound mice arises from the genetic interaction of VEGFR2 and ephrinB2 pathways
source: Importantly, single heterozygous VEGFR2 and ephrinB2 mice (Nes-cre Kdrlox/+ and Nes-cre Efnb2lox/+) showed a branching pattern that was undistinguishable from controls (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the phenotype observed arises from the genetic interaction of both pathways.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that single heterozygotes are normal but double heterozygotes show phenotype, indicating genetic interaction

claim: The density of dendritic spines of the Nes-cre Kdrlox/+ Efnb2lox/+ compound mice was reduced compared to controls littermates
source: Moreover, similar to the CA3 pyramidal neurons in Nes-cre Kdrlox/- mice, the density of dendritic spines of the Nes-cre Kdrlox/+ Efnb2lox/+compound mice was reduced compared to controls littermates (Figure 6F,G)
